member.name: T:ArchiMetrics.Analysis.CodeAnalysisAgent
member.summary: The facade over ArchiMetrics: wraps a Roslyn and exposes metrics, duplication detection and documentation analysis over it.

remarks.para: This is the type to use rather than the individual calculators. It exists because the analysis pipeline underneath has a lot of moving parts — compilations, semantic models, embedding providers — and wiring them correctly is not something every caller should have to learn.

Every query pages through skip/take and can be narrowed to one project. That is deliberate: it is designed to be driven by tools and coding agents, for which returning an entire solution's metric tree in one call is worse than useless.
Metric values are meaningless without their scale. See for the ranges, directions and rating bands, and use its Rate* methods rather than comparing against numbers of your own.

member.summary: Gets the lines of code.

remarks.para: Range: 0 and up. A size measure, not a quality measure — there is no good or bad value and no rating is derived from it.

These are real source lines: the lines the element occupies that carry code. Blank lines and comment-only lines are excluded, and so is documentation, so commenting a member does not make it measure larger. Lines holding only a brace are included, because a reader still scrolls past them.

At type level the figure is taken from the type's own declaration, so it includes the declaration line, the fields and the braces between members — it is therefore larger than the sum of its members' values, and that is intended. Namespace and project figures are the sums of the types beneath them.
Use this for anything the reader experiences as bulk. For the size input to the maintainability index, see — a figure that formatting cannot move.

member.name: P:ArchiMetrics.Analysis.Common.Metrics.ICodeMetric.ExecutableStatements
member.summary: Gets the number of executable statements — the units of work the code performs.

remarks.para: Range: 0 and up. Like this is a size measure with no good or bad value, but it counts syntax constructs rather than text. Formatting cannot change it: a statement wrapped over five lines still counts once, and braces and comments count for nothing. A member with no body at all — an interface method, an abstract declaration — scores 0.

That insensitivity to layout is why this, and not , is the size term in and the weight used when rolling member scores up into type, namespace and project figures. A metric that moved when only the whitespace changed would be worse than no metric.

Counted are statements (expression, if, switch, loops, using, lock, throw, yield, labelled, goto, checked, fixed, unsafe and empty statements), non-const local declarations, return only when it returns a value, an initializer as a single statement however many elements it holds, constructor declarations and expression-bodied accessors.
The result is not comparable with the Visual Studio metric of the same name. Use it to compare elements within a solution, not across tools.

member.name: P:ArchiMetrics.Analysis.Common.Metrics.ICodeMetric.MaintainabilityIndex
member.summary: Gets the maintainability index.

remarks.para: Range: 0 to 100, where higher is better. This is the normalised form of the index, not the raw Halstead-based formula that can go negative: results are scaled by 100 / 171 and clamped at 0, and a member with no measurable body scores 100.

The formula is MAX(0, (171 - 5.2 * ln(HalsteadVolume) - 0.23 * CyclomaticComplexity - 16.2 * ln(LinesOfCode)) * 100 / 171), so the index falls as a member grows in size, branching or vocabulary. It is a rough indicator of how hard a member is to read and change, and is best used to rank members against each other rather than as an absolute score.
For the band boundaries used across the library — healthy, concerning, and so on — see , and use to classify a value rather than hard-coding comparisons.

member.name: P:ArchiMetrics.Analysis.Common.Metrics.ICodeMetric.CyclomaticComplexity
member.summary: Gets the cyclomatic complexity.

remarks.para: Range: 1 and up, where lower is better. There is no upper limit. The value counts the linearly independent paths through the code: one for the body itself, plus one at every point where control flow can go more than one way.

Counted are if, all four loops, case labels (but not default:, which is the fall-through), catch clauses and their when filters, the short-circuiting && and ||, ?? and ??=, ?:, null-conditional access, each non-discard arm of a switch expression, and the and/or pattern combinators. Branches inside a lambda count towards the member that contains it.

Deliberately not counted: negation, default(T), continue and goto. None of them chooses between paths, and counting them penalised guard clauses — usually the more readable way to write the same logic.

The value is a lower bound on the number of test cases needed for full branch coverage, which is why high values are a testability problem rather than a style complaint. At type, namespace and project level it is aggregated from the members beneath, so it grows with size as well as with branching — compare elements of similar size.
See for the band boundaries. The result is not comparable with the Visual Studio metric of the same name.

member.name: T:ArchiMetrics.Analysis.ReferenceResolvers.ReferenceRepository
member.summary:
A reverse index of "which code refers to this symbol?", built once for a whole solution.
Answering that question on demand means asking Roslyn to bind the solution again for every symbol, which is quadratic: a few hundred classes times a few hundred documents. Binding every node exactly once up front and remembering the answers turns each later question into a dictionary lookup, which is the difference between minutes and seconds for a real solution.
Callers must await before calling . Get is a plain synchronous read on purpose: an earlier version blocked inside Get, and because every rule performs thousands of lookups, those blocked threads exhausted the thread pool and the analysis appeared to hang. Waiting is now something the caller does once, asynchronously, rather than something every lookup does implicitly.

member.name: F:ArchiMetrics.Analysis.SymbolExtensions.KnownReferences
member.summary:
One reference index per solution snapshot.
The table is keyed on the solution instance itself, which gives two properties for free. Roslyn treats a solution as immutable, so editing produces a new instance and therefore a new index - keying on the solution *id* instead would survive edits and hand back stale references. And because the table holds its keys weakly, an index disappears once the solution it describes is collected, so a long-lived host such as the analysis agent does not accumulate every solution it has ever opened.

member.name: M:ArchiMetrics.Analysis.SymbolExtensions.WarmReferenceIndex(Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Solution)
member.summary:
Builds the solution's reference index if it does not exist yet.
Call this once before analysing many symbols. The index is what makes reference lookups cheap, but building it is the single most expensive step, so it is better paid once up front than discovered concurrently by hundreds of callers.

member.name: M:ArchiMetrics.Analysis.SymbolExtensions.FindReferences(Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Solution,Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.ISymbol)
member.summary:
Looks a symbol up in the solution's shared reference index, building that index on first use.
Rules call this once per declaration, so a solution produces tens of thousands of lookups. That makes the cost of a single lookup the thing that matters: this used to wrap every one in a Task.Run that then blocked waiting for the index, so thousands of pool threads sat blocked on work that itself needed pool threads to finish, and the analysis stalled rather than ran. Awaiting the scan once and then reading straight from the dictionary keeps a lookup as cheap as it looks.
